title: Handoff contracts, kernel switchover, and KV staleness metrics
content:
Purpose and scope:
This doc collects the minimal runtime 'contract' that must be honored when we perform speculative decode handoffs between kernels, the observable signals we will use to gate acceptance for a new model/kernel combination, and a compact set of KV cache staleness metrics that are actionable for rollback decisions.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers implementing kernel switchover and handoff orchestration
- Oncall/SREs who will respond to regressions during canaries
- Applied ML for model acceptance criteria

High-level motivation (notes to self):
- Speculative decoding increases throughput but creates coupling across kernel implementations and KV cache semantics. We need a small surface area of guarantees to avoid correctness hazards (bad continuity, duplicated tokens, or silent drift).
- We also need a fast, automatable gate/rollback signal set that is robust to normal traffic variance and signal noise.

Contract primitives (what a new kernel/model variant must provide):
1) deterministic-token-boundary: given identical input prefix + RNG seed (when used), the kernel should produce a stable next-token distribution estimate for the first N tokens (N configurable, default 4). If a kernel uses nondeterministic heuristics, it must expose a seeded-mode for acceptance canaries.
2) kv-prefix-compatibility: the kernel must honor KV cache segment boundaries defined by the runtime (segment-size, versioning header). On mismatch, it must return a well-formed diagnostic code and accept a full-prefix-recompute path rather than silently treating the KV as opaque.
3) continuation-checksum: before handing off, the producing kernel writes a tiny continuation checksum (e.g., CRC32 over last 64 bytes of decode state + sequence id). The consumer kernel verifies; mismatch causes declared 'handoff-incompatibility' rather than undefined behavior.
4) graceful-fallback: consumer kernel must support an explicit fallback API to request a rerun on a compatible kernel when mismatch occurs.

Handoff sequence (optimistic path):
- runtime decides to handoff at token boundary T based on batching and latency heuristics
- producing kernel exports KV segment up to T and writes continuation-checksum + prefix-length + sequence-id
- router selects consumer kernel instance and transmits lightweight handshake (checksum + requested seeds + any attention-slicing hints)
- consumer verifies checksum, integrates KV segment, and returns ACK ready to resume
- producing kernel finalizes and releases locks; consumer resumes generation from T+1

Failure modes and runtime reactions (non-exhaustive):
- checksum mismatch -> increment metric handoff.checksum_mismatch; route request to fallback kernel variant; mark consumer instance unhealthy for 30s and collect debug snapshot
- kv-eviction mid-handshake -> record handoff.kv_eviction; trigger full-prefix-recompute path; if recompute added > Xms (configurable), consider race metric and throttle speculative handoffs for this model
- timeout waiting for ACK -> treat as transient; increment handoff.timeout and apply exponential backoff for that source pair

KV staleness metrics (definition and instrumentation):
- kv.segment_age_ms: time since a KV segment was written to the cache (per segment)
- kv.prefix_hit_rate_10m: fraction of requests whose full working prefix matched an existing cache segment within last 10m
- kv.recompute_rate: rate per-second of requests that fell back to full recompute due to incompatibility or eviction
- kv.handshake_latency_p95: P95 of time between producing kernel export and consumer ACK
- kv.staleness_impact_score: computed per-request as min(1.0, (recompute_cost_ms / expected_token_latency_ms)) aggregated as P99 over 5m windows (see notes below)
- Instrumentation tags: model, kernel-id, region, dedupe-group, request-path-id

Metric thresholds for automatic gating (initial proposal, conservative):
- handoff.checksum_mismatch rate > 0.02% over 15m -> fail canary and rollback
- kv.recompute_rate > 0.5% over 5m for traffic > 50rps -> fail canary
- handoff.handshake_latency_p95 > 120ms sustained over 10m -> pause handoffs and switch to single-kernel mode for that model
- kv.staleness_impact_score P99 > 2.0 -> investigate and hold rollout

Notes on those thresholds:
- numbers are intentionally conservative to avoid noisy rollbacks. We expect to tune with synthetic load tests and a handful of low-risk customers.
- thresholds should support graded responses: pause handoffs for one availability zone, reduce speculative handoff frequency, or full rollback.

Acceptance checklist for a new kernel/model variant (automatable items first):
- unit tests for deterministic-token-boundary and seeded-mode (PASS)
- handshake compliance test via local harness (PASS)
- synthetic traffic run: 1M requests with varied prefix lengths; recompute_rate < 0.05% AND continuity errors < 0.01%
- canary rollout: 1% traffic for 24h with the metric thresholds above enforced
- service-level smoke checks: end-to-end tests for stop/start and continuity over KV evictions
- observability: required logs/events exist: handoff.start, handoff.handshake, handoff.ack, handoff.mismatch, kv.segment_written, kv.segment_evicted

Rollback decision flow (fast path):
1) Alert triggers for threshold breach -> oncall page for serving-runtime receives incident
2) Quick triage: check handoff.* and kv.* metrics, look for correlated load or infra events
3) If checksum_mismatch or recompute_rate breach and steady for > 10m -> execute rollback to previous kernel variant for affected model + region using canary control plane
4) If handshake_latency_p95 breach but without errors -> throttle handoffs and revert to single-kernel generation path while investigating network/serialization latency
5) Post-rollback: capture deterministic trace for 1k failing requests for model team and attach to GH PR

Operational play (runbook snippets):
- To pause handoffs for model X in region R: POST /admin/models/X/handoff?action=pause-region&region=R with reason + escalation ticket
- Emergency rollback: PUT /admin/models/X/deployments?variant=previous&idempotent=true
- Collecting artifacts for incident: s3://redwood-debug/handoffs/{date}/{model}/{instance}/ and an automatic diagnostic bundle that includes KV headers, checksums, and last 8 tokens of state (redact user contents).

Debugging tips for SREs (quick):
- If handoff.checksum_mismatch spikes, try immediate local handshake test against the consumer instance using the debug handshake endpoint. If mismatch persists across many instances, it is likely a producer kernel bug or a versioning header change.
- If kv.recompute_rate is high but checksums are stable, check for frequent KV evictions: kv.segment_age_ms and k8s OOM events often coincide.
- Use the 'replay-and-compare' harness to reproduce nondeterministic token drift. Run with seeded-mode to force deterministic behavior.

Open questions (important to resolve before broad rollout):
- Should continuation-checksum be cryptographic (SHA256) or a lightweight CRC? Tradeoffs: crypto prevents deliberate tampering but costs CPU; CRC is faster and likely sufficient for accidental mismatches.
- How to version KV segment format so older consumers gracefully decline rather than silently misinterpret? Do we bake a semantic version header in the segment?
- Can we leverage existing kernel scheduling hints (attention-slice hints) to reduce handshake size without increasing coupling?
- How to include randomness seeds (for non-deterministic samplers) in the handshake without leaking user-level entropy?

Short-term action items (owner initials):
- (AC) implement continuation-checksum in runtime shim and wire basic handshake logs to metrics
- (PN) add kv.recompute_rate metric and dashboard tile for model-level breakdown
- (MS) create synthetic workload harness that exercises partial prefix handoffs and KV eviction scenarios
- (ER) draft incident runbook snippets for rollback endpoints and debug bundle format

Appendix: toy examples and scenarios
1) Small mismatch example:
- Producer wrote segment V1.0 header but consumer expects V1.1. Continuation-checksum fails -> consumer returns incompatibility. Runtime increments mismatch metric and routes fallback. This is safe and expected during rolling kernel upgrades.

2) Eviction race example:
- Producer exports KV, but before consumer ACK, segment is evicted due to memory pressure. Consumer requests segment and gets miss -> triggers full recompute. If recompute cost is small, runtime proceeds; if large and repeated, we should rate-limit handoffs and increase KV retention for model.

3) Network-induced latency example:
- Handshake p95 spikes due to serialization library regression. Observable in handshake_latency_p95 and increase in end-to-end tail latency but not in mismatch. Action: pause handoffs and roll serialization change.

Conversation/links to follow up:
- See GH PR redwood-inference/serving-runtime#3421 for early shim implementation notes
- See SRV-789 for the KV segment format proposal (attached)
- Slack thread #runtime-kernel-ops from Nov 8 for initial design feedback

Quick glossary:
- handoff: optimistic transfer of decode state and KV segment between two kernel instances to continue speculative decoding
- consumer/producer: consumer is the kernel that will continue generation; producer produced the last token(s)
- checksum: short verification piece written by producer and validated by consumer
- recompute: fallback path where decode state is regenerated from scratch without using a KV segment

End of draft.

Unpolished notes: there are many possible micro-optimizations (delta-compression for KV segments, resume tokens, layered checksums) but keep the first iteration simple and observable. We must avoid adding coupling that blocks a rollback.
